title: This one counts
hookLine: Epictetus: when you kiss your child, remember they are mortal (Discourses 3.24)

lines: ONE DAY, THIS WON'T BE HERE.
cards: It's bedtime. You lean over a sleeping child, or a partner, or an old dog curled on the rug, and for a second, out of nowhere, a thought arrives that you'd rather not have. One day, this won't be here.
Most of us flinch and push it away, as if thinking it might make it happen. Nearly two thousand years ago, Epictetus told his students something that shocked some of them. Don't push it away.
Let it come, right in the middle of the tenderest moment.

teach.b: In the Discourses, book three, Epictetus says, in paraphrase: when you kiss your child, what harm is there in whispering, tomorrow you may die? A student objects: that's ill-omened. You'll bring bad luck.
Epictetus answers: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested? Or that leaves fall in autumn? It's simply naming something that belongs to nature.
There's nothing unlucky in the truth.
In the Handbook he's briefer: when you kiss your child, remember you are kissing a human being, a mortal, so that if they die, you won't be shattered.
That's his own reason, and it's worth being honest about it: steadiness, loving what you have without pretending you'll have it forever. Some readers find that cold.
But many people who try the practice find something else inside it. The thought doesn't make them love less.
It makes the moment sharper. You don't take the goodnight for granted. You look a little longer.
You say the thing you were going to say tomorrow. That's the whole week, really. Marcus rose above the city and saw everyone at once.
Voyager showed one speck. The astronauts looked back. Memento mori, remember you will die.
Seneca rehearsed the loss so it couldn't ambush him. And Epictetus brings it all the way home, to one face, one hug, one ordinary evening. Not someday.

how: People who practice Stoicism sometimes follow Epictetus's advice from the Discourses and the Handbook: in a moment of affection, they quietly remember that the one they love is mortal, and let it deepen their attention.

o: a Stoic who taught remembering that loved ones are mortal
the Roman emperor who wrote the private Meditations
a Greek doctor who wrote on grief and how to heal it

games.q: what's inside Epictetus's lesson — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus said thinking of death brings bad luck
a student said so. Epictetus answered: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested?
Epictetus's own stated reason was steadiness, so a loss won't shatter you
many people who try it also find the moment grows sharper.
remembering someone is mortal makes you love them less
many find the opposite: you look longer, and don't take the goodnight for granted.

games.q: you're one of Epictetus's students. he's just told you to whisper tomorrow you may die while kissing your child. you think it's ill-omened. what does he answer?
o: you're right, forget I said it.
is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested?
then say it only in your head.
games.why: he compares it to the harvest and autumn leaves: naming something that belongs to nature. there's nothing unlucky in the truth.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love, a person or an animal, and picture their face. Let the true thought come, gently, they are mortal, and so am I, and notice what it does to how you see them.
Then picture the next time you'll greet them, and how you'd like to hold that moment.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus. The Stoic who told his students to remember, even while kissing someone they love, that they are mortal. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: look a little longer. Not someday; this goodnight. Day one hundred twenty-seven, done.
